Preamble
This document replaces the Leiden University PhD Guidelines 2023. The Protocol is
an independent scheme that contains information about the policy, arrangements
and facilities available with respect to the PhD programme. See also the Leiden
University PhD Regulations 2026, which contain the rules and procedures relating
to the dissertation and PhD programme.
The Protocol provides an overview of what PhD candidates can expect in terms of
training, supervision and facilities. The Protocol is binding. Attention is also paid to
facilities that apply not only to PhD candidates but to a broader group of (guest)
employees. Where applicable, this is indicated.
The Protocol applies to all types of PhD candidates (see 1.1). Where there are
exceptions, this is indicated. The (legal) position of the PhD candidate is governed
by the articles in the Collective Labour Agreement (CAO NU) that relate to a PhD
candidate with employment status.
2
1. General
1.1 Types of PhD candidates
Leiden University has the following types of PhD candidates (in accordance with
the UNL (Universities of the Netherlands) classification of types of PhD candidates,
as from 2019):
1. PhD candidates with employee status: employed PhD candidates
(werknemer-promovendi) and employees in a PhD track (promoverende
medewerkers) (UNL types 1a and 1b);
2. Scholarship-funded PhD candidates, who are not employed by Leiden
University or LUMC. Scholarship funded PhD candidates receive funding
from a scholarship funding body (UNL type 2);
3. Externally funded PhD candidates, who are not employed by Leiden
University or LUMC and do not receive a scholarship. These PhD candidates
may be employed by external research organisations or may be dual PhD
candidates who are writing a PhD dissertation with the support of their
employer (UNL type 3);
4. External PhD candidates (self-funded), not employed by Leiden University
or LUMC. External PhD candidates study towards a PhD in their free time and
use their own funds (UNL type 4).1
See Appendix 1 for a more detailed explanation of the types of PhD candidates.
1.2 Regulations, procedures and codes of conduct
The Leiden University PhD Regulations 2026 contain the most important rules and
procedures relating to the PhD track, such as who is permitted to defend a PhD,
what the tasks of the supervisors and co-supervisors are and what requirements
the dissertation must meet. PhD candidates and supervisors/co-supervisors are
required to read the PhD Regulations.
At Leiden University, the Golden Rules for PhD supervision serve as a code of
conduct for both the PhD candidate and the supervisors and co-supervisors. These
1
The Dual PhD Centre offers externally funded and external PhD candidates a range of facilities, for which it
charges a fee.
3
rules emphasise the shared responsibility of the supervisor/co-supervisor and the
PhD candidate, and make clear what their mutual expectations may be.
In addition, the PhD candidates must comply with the relevant general laws and
regulations, conditions and guidelines that apply within the university, LUMC,
faculty, Graduate School and institute, and those that focus specifically on the PhD
track and conducting PhD research. These relate to aspects including, but not
limited to: education requirements, academic freedom, academic integrity, open
science, data management, ethics review, environmental regulations, privacy and
personal, public and knowledge security.
4
2. Admission and registration
2.1 Admission
See Chapter 2 Procedure for admission to the PhD track of the PhD Regulations.
Institutes/faculties may impose additional requirements, such as a language
requirement for international PhD candidates. A knowledge security check applies
to the admission of international (guest) employees.
Admission of new PhD candidates takes place in consultation with the intended
supervisors and co-supervisors and others with responsibility within the institute
and/or faculty. New PhD candidates are only admitted if sufficient supervision time
and resources will be available throughout the entire envisioned PhD track.
Scholarship-funded PhD candidates may only be admitted if their monthly
scholarship is at least the ‘required income amount’ stipulated by the Immigration
and Naturalisation Service (IND). See the website of the IND for the current
required amount. Both the scholarship and monthly salary/bonus/supplements of a
facilitating employer or university may be counted in order to reach the required
amount, but the PhD candidate’s own funds, such as savings, may not be counted.
Scholarship funding bodies are expected to endorse Leiden University’s values
regarding academic freedom, academic integrity, open science, respectful culture
and knowledge security, and to provide transparency in relation to contracts
between the PhD candidate and the scholarship funding body, so that no conflicts
can arise between obligations towards the scholarship funding body and Dutch laws
and regulations and university regulations.
External PhD candidates from non-EEA countries must demonstrate that they have
sufficient personal funds (= 12 times the monthly IND required amount).
5
Graduate School
See Chapter 2, article 8 Admission to the Graduate School of the PhD Regulations. The
various Graduate Schools are:
• Graduate School of Archaeology
• Graduate School of Humanities
• Graduate School of Legal Studies
• Graduate School of Science
• Graduate School of Social and Behavioural Sciences
• Graduate School of Governance and Global Affairs
• Graduate School LUMC (PhD candidates of LUMC can also log in to
Albinusnet for more information)
2.2 Registration
At the start of their PhD track (starting date of employment contract or before or
immediately after the appointment of the supervisors and co-supervisors; articles
7.2 and 11 of the PhD Regulations), all PhD candidates are registered in the HRM
employee registration system of Leiden University or LUMC, as well as in the PhD
candidate monitoring system LUCRIS/Converis Graduate School Module (Converis
GSM). It is important that the applicable type of PhD candidate is entered here. The
categories of PhD candidate are described in 1.1.
LUCRIS/Converis GSM
This system is used by the PhD candidate and supervisors/co-supervisors to keep a
record of the various steps of the PhD track and to store relevant documentation in
one place. The Graduate School informs the PhD candidate how to register, what
information is required for this and how to log in. Please note that Leiden
University and LUMC each have their own Converis GSM system.
Manuals are available for PhD candidates and supervisors/co-supervisors:
• Supervisor’s Manual
• Researcher’s Manual
• FAQ
6
LUMC staff can make use of the information in Converis GSM: User manuals and
invormation - LUMC Research Information System
2.3 Payment of a fee
Leiden University has a central fee policy for scholarship providers. For externally
funded and external PhD candidates, fee policy may apply within the institute or
faculty. Contact the relevant For details and information on possible discounts or
waivers, please contact the relevant faculty or Graduate School for more
information and possible discounts or waivers.
2.4 PhD research at two universities
In some cases, PhD candidates may conduct research and be supervised at two
universities during their PhD track. It is important to formalise this collaboration
as early as possible in the process of the PhD track. More information can be found
here.
2.5 Duration of PhD track
For full-time PhD candidates with employee status and scholarship-funded PhD
candidates, the duration of a regular PhD track is in principle four years. In the case
of part-time employment, the employment contract will be extended
proportionally, as stated in the Collective Labour Agreement (CAO NU).
PhD tracks of externally funded and external PhD candidates may have a different
timeframe. They must have been registered with the Graduate School for at least
two years before the PhD defence takes place.
7
3. Training and supervision plan and data management
plan
3.1 Training and supervision plan
At the beginning of the PhD track, all PhD candidates must draw up a training and
supervision plan (TSP; opleidings- en begeleidingsplan OBP) in consultation with
their supervisors/co-supervisor(s). This will contain agreements about inter alia
supervision and academic and personal development. The TSP must be approved by
the supervisors/co-supervisors and uploaded in Converis GSM. PhD candidates
with employee status and scholarship-funded PhD candidates must do this within
three months following the formal start date of the PhD track (appointment
date/registration date). Externally funded and external PhD candidates must do it
within a maximum of six months following registration with the Graduate School.
The TSP can be updated, where applicable. At least once a year, the agreements in
the TSP, including training agreements, and the progress made in relation to these,
will be discussed during a progress interview or GROW interview (Conversations on
Performance, Development and Well-being).
The TSP will in any case, but not exclusively, include:
• Who will act as the supervisor/co-supervisor and who will provide any
further supervision, and also the content, scope and responsibilities of the
supervision and frequency of supervision contact occasions;
• The progress interviews and their scheduling:
• The GROW conversations for PhD candidates employed by the
university (the annual Conversations on Performance,
Development and Well-being). These are compulsory for PhD
candidates employed by the university. Other types of PhD
candidates affiliated to the university have at least one progress
interview per year;
• PhD candidates registered with the LUMC GS have at least an
annual progress interview. For PhD candidates who are also
employed by the LUMC, this may coincide with the annual
interview (if the timing is somewhat the same).
8
• The preparation for the 'go/no-go'moment and the time when the ‘go/no-
go’ decision will be made (see 6.4);
• The timeline of the research;
• Agreements about the structure of the dissertation;
• The individual training programme and the funding for this (courses,
training courses and conference attendances, see 5 in this protocol and
article 3 of the PhD Regulations);
• Teaching duties (if applicable, see 5.2).
• Agreements about intellectual property and what will happen with the
research data/results after the end of the PhD track (especially in case of
early termination).
The TSP may be different per faculty and/or institute.
3.2 Data management plan
All PhD candidates draw up a data management plan (DMP) for the PhD research,
following the guidelines of the faculty’s data management protocol. The faculty (or
other) data steward can provide support in this regard, and will also say where and
how the DMP should be kept. The DMP must be adjusted, when necessary.
The DMP contains a description of how the research data and software will be
managed, shared and documented during the PhD track, and the agreements and
conditions relating to their subsequent filing in a repository for long-term
management and storage. Leiden University has its own DMP template and we
recommend that you use it. This template is also accepted by most of the grant-
awarding bodies. Data management training courses are offered in the faculties and
at the Centre for Digital Scholarship. The faculty’s data management protocol must
be followed with regard to data management.
During the completion of the PhD track, the DMP must be supplemented with a
statement of what will happen to the research data at the end of the PhD track.
When research data from the PhD research has been published as a dataset in a data
repository, this dataset must be registered in Converis PM.
9
4. Facilities
The facilities offered may be different per type of PhD candidate and
faculty/institute. When admitting PhD candidates and during the PhD track, the
Graduate School and supervisors/co-supervisors should inform them about the
facilities that are (and are not) available to them, and the conditions for their use.
4.1 LU-Card
All PhD candidates are entitled to an LU-Card, which gives them, inter alia, access
to the library. See LU-Card for more information.
4.2 Copying and printing facilities
PhD candidates with employee status and scholarship-funded PhD candidates may
use copying and printing facilities without charge, in accordance with each
faculty’s rules for academic staff.
4.3 Workspace
PhD candidates with employee status and scholarship-funded PhD candidates are
entitled to a flexible (or regular) workspace in the faculty. Externally funded and
external PhD candidates can only be offered a workspace if the capacity of the
relevant faculty or institute permits this.
4.4 Conference attendance
PhD candidates with employee status and scholarship-funded PhD candidates are
given the opportunity, within reason, to attend at least two academic conferences
during their PhD track (with time and funding made available for this).
4.5 Insurance
All employees and guest employees are covered by Leiden University's liability
insurance while within the buildings and grounds of Leiden University. If they are
10
on a mission/fieldwork as part of their work (on behalf of the University and with
the permission of their supervisor), they are insured under the University's
business travel insurance. PhD candidates must coordinate their mission/fieldwork
with their supervisor(s).
4.6 Research support
The Leiden Research Support Portal gives access to information about research
support during all phases of the PhD (or other) research. A few important kinds of
support are highlighted here:
• The Leiden University Libraries offer a wide range of support to PhD
candidates in the areas of data, research and publishing.
• Each faculty has one or more ethics committees. PhD research must in any
event be submitted for ethical review if it will involve working with human
participants or respondents and/or if personal data will be processed.
• A privacy officer (or privacy contact person) can help with questions about
privacy and data protection when processing personal data. A security officer
(or LISO) can help if you have questions about information security. See the
list of privacy and security officers.
• Within Leiden University we work according to the Knowledge Security
policy framework. If you have any questions in this area, please contact the
knowledge security contact person in the faculty or the Knowledge Security
Advice Desk at adviespuntkv@bb.leidenuniv.nl.
• Information about ICT and research can be found here.
• You can contact the graduate school to check whether the PhD candidate is
eligible for a contribution towards costs related to the PhD defence.
4.7 Career support
PhD candidates and supervisors/co-supervisors are expected to regularly exchange
ideas on the next career steps within and outside the academic world. Leiden
University also has a PhD Career Platform, offering self-reflection and personality
tests, online courses, tips and alumni’s experiences. The Graduate Schools
regularly organise PhD Career Events. Leiden University also has several career
coaches who can assist PhD candidates with employee status and scholarship-
funded PhD candidates.
11
4.8 Well-being
PhD candidates who have questions or problems may contact, for example:
• A supervisor/co-supervisor (e.g. for questions/problems about the PhD
programme);
• Colleagues (e.g. for sparring and advice);
• In some faculties: counsellors, coordinators or mentors for PhD candidates
(e.g. to discuss problems within the PhD process);
• The confidential counsellor for PhD candidates and other confidential
counsellors (e.g. in the event of problems with supervision or colleagues,
disagreement about the direction of the research, an unsafe working
atmosphere, concerns about work-life balance);
• The psychologist for PhD candidates (in the event of psychological
complaints that are caused by the PhD process or have an effect on the PhD
process, e.g. stress complaints, burnout, motivation problems;
• The Ombuds Officer (in the event of problems within the working
environment).
The PNN (network for PhD candidates in the Netherlands) has developed a
roadmap.
4.9 Sick leave
PhD candidates with employee status
PhD candidates with employee status can find information here about reporting
sick and guidance during sick leave. In the event of illness, the employment
contract is not automatically extended. Supervisors must inform the PhD candidate
of any available possibilities.
PhD candidates without employee status
PhD candidates without an employment contract should report their absence to
their supervisor(s)/co-supervisor(s) in the event of sickness. They will then discuss
the expected duration of absence, cancellation of/approach to planned
arrangements, which tasks can perhaps still be performed, and maintaining
12
contact. If the sick leave continues for more than eight weeks, the
supervisor(s)/co-supervisor(s) are asked to inform the institute. In the case of
long-term sickness, the PhD candidate and supervisor(s)/co-supervisor(s) will
together look at the possible options for completing the PhD track. After recovery,
the training and supervision plan will be revised, if necessary.
It should be noted that supervisors/co-supervisors are also not permitted to ask
PhD candidates without an employment contract about the nature or cause of the
sickness.
4.10 Pregnancy
PhD candidates with employee status are entitled to maternity leave. More
information can be found here. An application for maternity leave should be
submitted via the Service Portal.
13
5. Training
5.1 Training plan
Every PhD candidate produces a training plan as part of the TSP in consultation
with the supervisor(s) (see 3.1c). The TSP, including the training plan, is approved
and adopted by the supervisor.
All PhD candidates with employee status and scholarship-funded PhD candidates
are required to complete a minimum of 140 hours of funded scientific training
activities and 140 hours of funded transferable skills training activities, including at
least one training course in the area of scientific integrity.
Externally funded and external PhD candidates are required to follow at least a
scientific integrity course and any courses that are specified as compulsory for the
faculty and/or institute. It must also be established, in consultation with the
supervisor(s)/co-supervisor(s), whether and, if so, what additional training is
needed to enable them to properly carry out their PhD research. If necessary they
will be given the opportunity to follow two other training courses funded by the
faculty/institute, in addition to any compulsory training courses.
Completed training hours must be recorded in Converis/GSM.
Transferable skills
There is not an exhaustive list of training courses, activities and skills that are
classed under ‘transferable skills’. As long as the training course or activity can
make a clear contribution to the PhD track and/or developments after obtaining the
PhD, within our outside the academic world, it may be regarded as a transferable
skill. The range can be very wide. A non-exhaustive list of examples is given here;
training courses in the areas of:
• Resilience;
• Leadership skills;
• Various forms of oral and written communication;
• Writing grant applications / funding acquisition;
• Project management;
14
• Time management;
• Data management;
• Academic integrity;
• Open science;
• Job application skills;
• Publishing, copyright, IP, etc.;
• Entrepreneurship;
• Networking;
• Career support / career planning;
• Language training;
• Active bystander;
• University Teaching Qualification (BKO) and 20 hours of teaching;
• Introductory and onboarding activities.
For transferable skills, PhD candidates can make use of the courses offered by HR
Learning & Development. See the Transferable Skills Programme Page. They can
also take training courses outside the university (for instance at National Research
Schools), as long as funding is available for this within the relevant faculty or
institute.
5.2 Teaching duties
For PhD candidates with employee status, the agreements relating to the PhD track
may include teaching duties. Agreements about teaching, and following training
courses in this area, must be included in the TSP. According to the Collective Labour
Agreement (CAO NU), the teaching effort of a PhD candidate with a four-year
employment contract may not exceed 20% of the employment. PhD candidates who
teach have the opportunity to obtain the Partial University Teaching Qualification
(BKO-deelcertificaat). In some cases, if it fits into the planning of the PhD
programme, a full University Teaching Qualification can also be obtained. This
must be determined in consultation with the supervisors. Only PhD candidates with
an employment contract are permitted to perform teaching duties. PhD candidates
without an employment contract are only permitted to give guest classes (and only
a few of these).
15
6. Supervision
6.1 Supervisory team
Each PhD candidate has at least two supervisors. See Chapter 3 of the PhD
Regulations for the tasks of the supervisor and co-supervisor. The TSP includes the
division of tasks between the supervisors. When the supervision is provided by two
institutes or two faculties, unambiguous agreements are made about the
distribution of the costs and benefits.
6.2 Supervision
In contacts between supervisors/co-supervisors and PhD candidates, the Golden
Rules for PhD Supervision will be observed.
The advice offered in the UNL document Healthy Practices in the Dutch PhD System
2.0 is that PhD candidates should meet with one of their supervisors/co-
supervisors at least once a month. However, supervision needs to be specifically
tailored to individuals. Supervisors/co-supervisors and PhD candidates agree
together how this should be designed. The form, content and intensity of the
supervision may be different per discipline, phase in the PhD track and type of PhD
candidate. The minimum requirement specified is that PhD candidates with
employee status and scholarship funded PhD candidates will have a supervision
meeting with one of their supervisors/co-supervisors at least ten times a year, and
with the whole supervisory team twice a year. This may also be in the form of a
progress interview. External PhD candidates and externally funded PhD candidates
will have a supervision meeting with one of their supervisors/co-supervisors at
least four times a year, and with the whole supervisory team once a year. This may
also be in the form of a progress interview.
Email communication between a supervisor/co-supervisor and PhD candidate
must take place via the university email address.
The quality of the supervision of PhD candidates is a recurring topic in the GROW
interview conducted with each supervisor/co-supervisor by their own manager.
16
6.3 Training for supervisors
Everyone who will be supervising PhD candidates for the first time is required to
follow or have followed the Supervising PhD Candidates course or a comparable
training. Additionally, everyone who is promoted from university lecturer
(UD/assistant professor) to senior university lecturer (UHD/associate professor) is
required to follow this course within a year. Completing this course is a
precondition for senior university lecturers who wish to obtain ius promovendi. This
course can be followed via HR Learning & Development. The course is also available
for other supervisors. There is a separate course for more experienced supervisors.
6.4 ‘Go/no-go’ interview
A ‘go/no-go’ interview is conducted with each PhD candidate, focusing on the
decision regarding whether or not the PhD track will continue (possibly under
certain conditions). The expectations of the PhD candidate and supervisors/co-
supervisors will also be further discussed. The decision must be substantiated and
must be part of a longer and transparent assessment process. The decision should
therefore never come as a surprise for the PhD candidate. It will be based on the
(updated) research proposal, the progress of the PhD track up to that time, and the
level of confidence in its successful completion. The decision and substantiation
will be set down in writing and carefully archived.
The format, input and timing of the go/no-go interview may be different per
Graduate School. The interview for PhD candidates with a four-year appointment
and scholarship funded PhD candidates usually takes place nine months after the
start of the PhD track. For PhD candidates with a longer appointment, externally
funded and external PhD candidates, it is usually half-way through the second
year, but no later than the end of the second year. In some Graduate Schools the
interview may also be attended by the PhD dean or PhD coordinator and/or an
external evaluator, in addition to the PhD candidate and supervisors/co-
supervisors. In view of the sensitivity and importance of the interview, and the
emotional implications for the PhD candidate, it is advisable to always ensure that a
neutral person is present (who is not a member of the supervisory team). This role
is fulfilled at the LUMC by the Guidance Committee.
If the decision is made to terminate the PhD track, at least the following actions
must be taken:
17
• The supervisor sends written confirmation to the PhD candidate.
• The supervisor(s)/co-supervisor(s) schedule and conduct an exit interview.
This will include discussion of what will happen with the research data.
• The supervisor(s)/co-supervisor(s) inform HR.
• The supervisor(s) inform the Graduate School about the termination and the
reason for the termination.
• The supervisor changes the PhD track in Converis GSM to ‘early
termination’.
• If a scholarship is involved, the funding body needs to be informed. Who will
do this (PhD candidate or (co-)supervisor) depends on the applicable
agreements with the funding body.
• The PhD candidate should be given enough time to prepare for departure,
such as cancelling rent and insurances, organising the return journey, etc.
• If applicable, the supervisor/co-supervisor can write a recommendation
letter.
6.5 Progress interviews
A progress interview will take place at least once a year with every PhD candidate.
This will also include discussion of progress with the training programme.
Agreements that are made in this interview should be carefully documented and
archived (for instance in Converis GSM). In some institutes/faculties this interview
is also attended by a Supervision Committee/Guidance Committee. For PhD
candidates who have a GROW interview, this can be combined with the progress
interview. The Golden Rules for PhD Supervision are a useful resource for this
interview.
The way in which the progress interview is organised may be different per type of
PhD candidate and institute/faculty. It is a shared responsibility of the
supervisors/co-supervisors and the PhD candidate to ensure that progress
interviews take place.
6.6 Monitoring meeting
All PhD candidates are given the opportunity to have a review meeting/monitoring
meeting with one or two independent staff members (at which the supervisors/co-
supervisors are not present). The quality of the supervision will be an important
18
topic in this meeting. The independent staff member(s) will take follow-up action
if the meeting gives cause for this. This role is fulfilled at the LUMC by the Guidance
Committee.
PhD candidates with employee status and scholarship-funded PhD candidates must
be invited to a monitoring meeting every year. Externally funded and external PhD
candidates must be invited at least once every two years, although it is not
compulsory for them to accept this invitation.
6.7 Major change in supervision during the PhD track
The PhD Regulations provide for the possibility of making major changes in the
supervision during the PhD track. The basic principle is that, as soon as possible,
clear agreements should be made, set down in writing and shared with the
Graduate School. When making these agreements, the PhD candidate’s interest has
substantial weight.
There are two standard situations that we regard as major changes in the
supervision structure, namely if the first supervisor retires (becomes emeritus) or
accepts a chair at another university.
In these two cases, it is always essential to discuss whether a change in the
supervision structure is desirable or necessary. The deliberations should in any case
take account of the expected duration of the remaining PhD track and who will be
appointed to the chair. The departing professor will draw up a plan, based on
discussions with the people concerned, and discuss this plan with their own
manager. If the professor supervises several PhD tracks, all the various
arrangements should be discussed at the same time. After an agreement has been
reached, the Graduate School and the Dean of the faculty must be informed.
A further aspect of accepting a chair at another university is that agreements about
scholarships or research funding will be made. Financial agreements of this kind
may not be detrimental to earlier agreements between the supervisor and PhD
candidate. The PhD candidate has an employment contract or guest appointment at
Leiden University or LUMC that continues to be applicable and the PhD candidate
retains the opportunity to continue the PhD track within that employment contract.
If the PhD candidate expresses a wish to follow the professor who is departing, the
Graduate School will cooperate with this.
19
New agreements on guidance will be included in the TSP.
Another consideration if the professor becomes emeritus is that the period of
emeritus status is intended for finalising current PhD tracks. Although presented as
a possibility in the PhD Regulations, starting new PhD tracks as the first supervisor
during the final period before becoming emeritus is not recommended. See policy
on professorial appointments.
See also Policy on Professorial Appointments.
20
7. Copyright, intellectual property and open access
publishing
7.1 Copyright
The PhD candidate holds the copyright on the dissertation and other publications of
the PhD candidate, regardless of whether the research was conducted individually
by the PhD candidate or together with other Leiden University employees,
including the supervisor(s)/co-supervisor(s). If part of the dissertation (e.g. a
chapter) is written jointly with other authors, the copyright on that part of the
dissertation belongs to the PhD candidate and the other authors jointly. See
Employer Copyright Regulations - Leiden University.
7.2 Intellectual property
In the case of PhD candidates with employee status, all the intellectual property
developed during the PhD track (other than the copyright referred to in 7.1) belongs
to Leiden University as the employer. See Employer Copyright Regulations - Leiden
University.
For PhD candidates without an employment contract, all the intellectual property
developed during the PhD track belongs to the PhD candidate, if the research was
conducted individually. If the PhD candidate receives funding from an external
party, the ownership depends on the agreements made with the funder.
With respect to an invention, a PhD candidate without an employment contract
may choose to make use of the Regulations on Knowledge Exploitation. For this,
please contact Luris via ip@luris.nl.
If research is conducted together with researchers employed by Leiden University,
all the intellectual property (including knowhow or an invention) that was
developed in co-creation with Leiden University employees is owned by Leiden
University.
21
7.3 Open access
Leiden University encourages PhD candidates to publish on an open access basis,
and facilitates this. Even if they do not publish with open access, the university
expects PhD candidates to make short academic works openly available in the
Leiden Repository six months after their online publication. The dissertation must
be included in the Leiden Repository. This can be done via Converis GSM. The PhD
candidate must give the university a licence for non-exclusive publication of the
dissertation in digital format, if necessary under a temporary embargo.
Established by the Executive Board on July 14, 2026

UNL categorisation as of 2019
Each year, UNL asks the Dutch universities to submit their data on their PhD
candidates. These data are used as benchmarks for the association's own member
universities and for nationwide statistics and are published on UNL's website.
There are many different ways in which people can be awarded doctorates. The
universities and UMCs distinguish four types of PhD candidates. Definitions of the
various types of PhD candidates can help the universities correctly register their
PhD candidates, thus allowing the universities to submit high-quality data.
Categorisation involves a flow chart that helps universities assign PhD candidates
to the right category.
The distinctions between the categories were defined in greater detail because
there was some confusion as to the phrases 'contracted PhD candidates' and
'external PhD candidates' and as to the categorisation of candidates who are
employed by a university or UMC but are not allotted any hours or funding to work
on their dissertations. The new categorisation system comes with new, clearer
names, and the distinctions between the various types of PhD candidates depend on
the source of the funding the PhD candidate receives. This distinction does not
always provide the right definition, but does largely determine the extent to which
a university or UMC is aware of the PhD candidate.
Lastly, it should be pointed out that as far as statistics are concerned, PhD
candidates are always assigned to their primary category (which is the one in which
they were initially registered), even if their status later changes. Employee PhD
candidates will continue to be registered as employee PhD candidates, even if they
do some of their work on their dissertation outside the scope of an employment
contract with the university or UMC, while PhD candidates who do not receive any
funding or resources from a university or UMC will continue to belong to that
category, even if, due to temporary funding, such PhD candidates are able to
conduct research at a university or UMC for a while.

Category 1: PhD candidates employed by the university or UMC
1a Employee PhD candidates
An employee who has an employment contract with their own university, and for
whom arrangements have been made designed to help them complete a doctoral
research project.
Indicators:
a. Arrangements designed to help the PhD candidate complete a doctoral
research project (access to graduate school, training and supervision
plan, research plan, the assignment of a supervisor and doctoral
advisers).
b. Employee ID number and salary paid by the university or UMC > 0.
c. Primary UFO code is 'PhD candidate' or the UMC equivalent thereof.
This category also includes PhD candidates who were already employed by the
university or UMC at any point prior to starting their doctoral research, even if their
contract had expired by the time they commenced their doctoral research.
1b Employees who are conducting doctoral research
An employee who has an employment contract with their own university, and for
whom arrangements have been made designed to help them complete a doctoral
research project.
Indicators:
a. Arrangements designed to help the PhD candidate complete a doctoral
research project (access to graduate school, training and supervision plan,
research plan, the assignment of a supervisor).
b. Employee ID number and salary paid by the university or UMC > 0.
c. Primary UFO code is something other than 'PhD candidate' or the UMC
equivalent thereof.
This will be a PhD candidate who has been allotted funding and/or hours by their
university or UMC to conduct doctoral research. This category includes medical
specialists whose regular hours at the UMC are reduced to allow them to conduct
24
doctoral research. Employees who are working towards a doctorate without funding
and who are not allotted any hours by their university or UMC to conduct their
doctoral research fall under category no. 4.
In some cases, a secondary UFO code pertaining to the same appointment may
come with the 'PhD candidate' code. Or alternatively, one person may have two
employment relationships, one of which is employee PhD candidate.
UNL uses the following algorithm to determine which is the primary employment
relationship:
a. Whichever employment relationship carries the greatest FTE allocation is
considered the primary employment relationship.
b. If both employment relationships have the same FTE allocation, a
permanent contract takes precedence over a temporary one.
c. If both employment relationships come with the same type of contract, the
one with the higher pay scale takes precedence.
d. If both employment relationships come with the same pay scale, the UFO
code with the lowest number takes precedence.
e. If none of these rules results in an outcome, the employment relationship
that is first listed in the WOPI file (i.e., the employment relationship that
commenced first) will be considered the primary employment relationship.
Categories 2, 3 and 4: PhD candidates NOT employed by the university or UMC
2 Scholarship-funded PhD candidates2
These are PhD candidates who are not on an employment contract with the
university where they are completing their doctoral research, but whose main
objective is to obtain a doctorate, and who have been awarded funding by a third
party to do so.
Indicators:
a. Arrangements designed to help the PhD candidate complete a doctoral
research project (access to graduate school, training and supervision plan,
research plan, the assignment of a supervisor).
b. No salary paid by the university or UMC (except perhaps a supplement to the
third-party grant).

c. The PhD candidate receives funding from a third party for the purpose of
obtaining a doctorate.
The grant is provided by an organisation other than the university within the
meaning of section 2a, e.g. NUFFIC, the European Union, a foreign university,
granting agencies and foundations (Fullbright, banks). The PhD candidate may
receive a supplemental grant from their own university or UMC.
3 PhD candidates who receive external funding
PhD candidates who receive external funding differ from external PhD candidates
in that they either receive funding to conduct doctoral research or have been
allotted time by their boss to conduct doctoral research (regardless of the amount
of time they have been allotted).
4 External PhD candidates (self-funded)
These are PhD candidates who are not allotted any hours or funding to conduct
doctoral research by an external party but do wish to obtain a doctorate. They fund
their own research, or use funding placed at their disposal by their relatives. For
example: a pensioner who conducts doctoral research, an employee of a company
who conducts doctoral research on their own time on top of their regular job, a
university employee
whose UFO profile does not say 'PhD candidate' and who is not allotted any hours
or funding by the university to conduct their research either (formerly known as
'employees seeking to obtain a doctorate'), or a medical specialist whose UMC is
not reducing their regular hours to allow them to conduct doctoral research.
Indicators:
a. Arrangements designed to help the PhD candidate complete a doctoral
research project (access to graduate school, training and supervision plan,
research plan, the assignment of a supervisor).
b. No salary or grant paid by the university or UMC.
c. No funding and/or hours allotted by an employer or third party (including
the PhD candidate's own university) to allow the candidate to conduct their
research.
